title: Physical Chemistry Laboratory
description: The standard physical chemistry lab experiments: the theory behind each, how it is run, how the data is analyzed, the typical results and the main sources of error. Starts with the data analysis used in every report.

entries.name: Data analysis, error propagation and curve fitting
entries.tagline: The statistics every physical chemistry report needs.

points: Random errors scatter the results about the true value. They affect precision and can be reduced by repeating and averaging.
Systematic errors push all results the same way, such as a miscalibrated thermometer. They affect accuracy, do not average out, and have to be found and corrected.
Precision is the closeness of repeated results to each other. Accuracy is closeness to the true value.

sections.text: For n = 5 measurements, the Student t value at 95% confidence is 2.776 (4 degrees of freedom). The standard deviation describes the scatter of the data, and the standard error the uncertainty of the mean.

points: Sums and differences: add the absolute uncertainties in quadrature, σ = √(σ₁² + σ₂²).
Products and quotients: add the relative uncertainties in quadrature, σ_f/f = √((σ₁/x₁)² + (σ₂/x₂)²).
Powers: for f = xⁿ, σ_f/f = |n| σ_x/x.

General: σ_f² = Σ (∂f/∂xᵢ)² σᵢ². Example: density ρ = m/V with m = 5.00 ± 0.01 g and V = 2.00 ± 0.02 mL gives relative uncertainties of 0.2% and 1%, so σ_ρ/ρ = √(0.002² + 0.01²) ≈ 1.0%. The volume dominates, so improving the balance would not help.

Linearize the equation so that a plot is straight, then do a least-squares fit for the slope and intercept and their standard errors. Examples: ln k against 1/T (Arrhenius), ln p against 1/T (Clausius–Clapeyron), absorbance against concentration (Beer's law), 1/[A] against t (second-order kinetics).
Always look at a residual plot. A pattern, such as a curve, means the model is wrong. Random scatter means the line is adequate.
R² alone does not show that the fit is good. When points have unequal uncertainties, use a weighted fit. Linearization also changes the weights of points.
Spreadsheet functions such as LINEST give the uncertainties of the slope and intercept.

sections.text: Give the result with its uncertainty, with the uncertainty to one or two significant figures, and the result to the same decimal place. For example, ΔH = −41.3 ± 0.8 kJ/mol. Compare with the literature value, and say whether the difference is within the uncertainty. If not, discuss systematic errors.

quiz.q: How are the uncertainties combined when two measured quantities are multiplied?
quiz.a: Add their relative uncertainties in quadrature

quiz.q: What does a curved pattern in a residual plot show?
quiz.a: The model does not fit the data

entries.name: Experiment: heat of combustion by bomb calorimetry
entries.tagline: Measuring the energy of a fuel with a sealed bomb, and converting ΔU to ΔH.

sections.text: A weighed sample is burned in oxygen in a constant-volume bomb, and the heat released raises the temperature of the calorimeter. The heat released at constant volume is the internal energy change ΔU, not ΔH.

points: Calibration: burn a pellet of benzoic acid, whose heat of combustion is known very precisely (−26.43 kJ/g). The calorimeter constant is C_cal = (heat released) ÷ ΔT. A typical value is about 10 kJ/K.

Burn a weighed pellet of the sample, for example naphthalene (ΔcU about −5157 kJ/mol). Load it with a measured length of fuse wire, add 20–30 atm of oxygen, and place the bomb in a known mass of water in an insulated jacket.
Record the water temperature every 30 seconds before ignition (the fore period), during the rapid rise and afterwards (the after period).
ΔT is found by extrapolating the fore and after periods back to the time of ignition on a graph, to correct for heat exchange with the surroundings.
Corrections: the heat from the burning fuse wire, and the formation of nitric acid from the nitrogen in the air in the bomb. The nitric acid is found by titrating the washings of the bomb.
For naphthalene, C₁₀H₈(s) + 12O₂ → 10CO₂ + 4H₂O(l), Δn(gas) = 10 − 12 = −2, so ΔH = ΔU − 2RT = ΔU − 4.96 kJ/mol at 298 K.
Typical precision is about 0.3–0.5%.

sections.text: Incomplete combustion (soot, which means a failed run), heat exchange with the room, an inaccurate fuse wire correction, a thermometer error, moisture in the sample, and not equilibrating the temperature before ignition.

quiz.q: A bomb calorimeter directly measures the change in…
Why is benzoic acid used in the calibration?
quiz.a: Its heat of combustion is known very accurately
wrong: It does not need a fuse

entries.name: Experiment: vapor pressure and enthalpy of vaporization
entries.tagline: Measuring how vapor pressure rises with temperature to get ΔH_vap.

sections.text: From the Clausius–Clapeyron equation, a plot of ln p against 1/T for a liquid is a straight line with slope −ΔH_vap/R.

points: An isoteniscope holds a small sample of the liquid, connected to a manometer and a vacuum line, in a thermostat bath.
The liquid is degassed by gentle boiling to remove dissolved air, which would add to the pressure.

At each of 5–7 temperatures, for example from 20 to 60 °C, the pressure on the outside is adjusted until the liquid levels on the two sides of the isoteniscope are equal. The external pressure then equals the vapor pressure.
Plot ln p against 1/T (T in kelvin), fit a line, and find ΔH_vap = −R × slope, with its uncertainty from the fit.
For water the result is usually about 41–44 kJ/mol, compared with 40.7 kJ/mol at the boiling point. Because ΔH_vap decreases with temperature, a slight curvature is expected over a wide range.
Trouton's rule: for many non-polar liquids, ΔS_vap = ΔH_vap/T_b is about 88 J/(mol·K). It is higher for water (about 109) and other hydrogen-bonded liquids because the liquid is more ordered.

sections.text: Air left in the sample, a thermometer that is not calibrated or that reads a different temperature from the sample, leaks in the vacuum line, and the pressure gauge. Using only a narrow temperature range makes the slope uncertain.

quiz.q: In a vapor pressure experiment, what is plotted to find ΔH_vap?

entries.name: Experiment: freezing point depression and molar mass
terms: molar mass by freezing point depression
entries.tagline: Finding the molar mass of an unknown solute from how much it lowers a solvent's freezing point.

equations: M = K_f × (mass of solute) ÷ (ΔT_f × kg of solvent)
sections.text: A solute lowers the freezing point in proportion to its molality, whatever the solute (a colligative property). K_f is a property of the solvent. Cyclohexane has T_f = 6.5 °C and K_f = 20.0 °C·kg/mol, which is large, so the effect is easy to measure.

points: Record a cooling curve of the pure solvent: temperature against time while stirring, in an ice bath.
Add a weighed amount of the solute and repeat.

The freezing point is found from the plateau. A liquid often supercools below its freezing point before crystals form, and the temperature then jumps back up to the true freezing point. To correct this, extrapolate the cooling line back to where it meets the plateau.

sections.text: 0.50 g of an unknown dissolved in 20.0 g of cyclohexane lowers the freezing point by 0.80 °C. Molality = 0.80 ÷ 20.0 = 0.040 mol/kg, so moles of solute = 0.040 × 0.0200 = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol, and M = 0.50 ÷ 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 625 g/mol.

points: Supercooling, and heat from stirring, which makes the plateau not flat.
The solute may dissociate (van 't Hoff factor i > 1) or associate (i < 1), such as carboxylic acids dimerizing in a non-polar solvent, which would give a molar mass twice as large.
Evaporation of the solvent, moisture entering, and the thermometer resolution. At high concentration, the solution is not ideal.

quiz.q: A carboxylic acid dimerizes in cyclohexane. What happens to the molar mass found by freezing point depression?
quiz.a: It appears about twice as large

entries.name: Experiment: binary phase diagrams
entries.tagline: Mapping out melting behavior of a two-component mixture from cooling curves.

sections.text: In a solid–liquid phase diagram of two components that are miscible as liquids but not as solids, the freezing point of each component falls as the other is added, until the two curves meet at the eutectic point, the lowest temperature at which any liquid exists. The eutectic mixture freezes at one temperature, like a pure compound.

points: Melt a series of mixtures of different compositions, for example lead and tin, bismuth and tin, or naphthalene and biphenyl.
Record the temperature against time as each cools slowly.
A pure component shows a flat plateau at its freezing point. A mixture shows a break in slope when the first solid forms, then a slower cooling rate, then a plateau at the eutectic temperature.
Plot the break temperature and the plateau temperature against composition to build the diagram.
The length of the eutectic plateau is longest at the eutectic composition (a Tammann plot), which locates it. For Pb–Sn it is 61.9% Sn at 183 °C and for Bi–Sn 58% Bi at 139 °C.
Gibbs phase rule at constant pressure: F = C − P + 1. At the eutectic, with two solids and a liquid present, F = 0, so the temperature is fixed during the plateau.
The lever rule gives the proportions of the phases at any point inside a two-phase region.

sections.text: In a partly miscible pair, such as phenol and water, the solubility curve has an upper critical solution temperature, the temperature above which they mix in all proportions (about 66 °C at about 34% phenol by mass). It is found by heating a sealed tube until it clears.

quiz.q: How many degrees of freedom are there at a eutectic point at constant pressure for a two-component system?

entries.name: Experiment: equilibrium constant by spectrophotometry (FeSCN²⁺)
entries.tagline: Using the color of a complex ion to find the concentrations at equilibrium.

sections.text: The FeSCN²⁺ complex is blood red and absorbs at about 447 nm, while the reactants are nearly colorless there. So the absorbance gives the equilibrium concentration of the complex.

points: Calibration: mix a small amount of SCN⁻ with a large excess of Fe³⁺ (for example 0.2 M) so that essentially all the SCN⁻ becomes FeSCN²⁺. Then [FeSCN²⁺] equals the initial [SCN⁻], and A = ε b c gives the molar absorptivity ε.
Prepare a series of mixtures with known initial concentrations of Fe³⁺ and SCN⁻ at constant temperature in dilute nitric acid, and measure A.
Keep the acid at about 0.1–1 M to prevent the hydrolysis of Fe³⁺ to Fe(OH)²⁺, which is also colored, and keep the ionic strength constant.
[FeSCN²⁺]ₑq = A ÷ (εb).
[Fe³⁺]ₑq = [Fe³⁺]₀ − [FeSCN²⁺]ₑq, and [SCN⁻]ₑq = [SCN⁻]₀ − [FeSCN²⁺]ₑq (an ICE table).
K_c is calculated for each mixture, and the values are averaged. It is of the order of 10²–10³ M⁻¹ under these conditions, and the values should agree within a few percent.

sections.text: In the method of continuous variations, the total concentration is held constant while the mole fraction of each reactant is varied. The absorbance of the complex peaks at the mole fraction that corresponds to the stoichiometry, 0.5 for a 1:1 complex.
Formation of Fe(SCN)₂⁺ at high thiocyanate, a drift in temperature (K depends on T), cuvette handling and dilution errors, and the slow decomposition of the complex in light.

quiz.q: In Job's method, the maximum absorbance of a 1:1 complex occurs at a mole fraction of…

entries.name: Experiment: reaction kinetics (crystal violet and iodine clock)
entries.tagline: Finding rate laws and activation energies from two classic reactions.

sections.text: Crystal violet (CV⁺, purple) reacts with hydroxide to give a colorless product. The rate law is rate = k[CV⁺][OH⁻].
points: With hydroxide in large excess, [OH⁻] is constant and the reaction is pseudo-first-order: rate = k′[CV⁺], where k′ = k[OH⁻].
Monitor the absorbance at about 590 nm in a spectrophotometer. A plot of ln A against time is a straight line with slope −k′.
Varying [OH⁻] and plotting ln k′ against ln [OH⁻] gives the order in hydroxide (1).
Repeating at several temperatures and plotting ln k against 1/T gives the activation energy by the Arrhenius equation.

A small, known amount of thiosulfate is added with starch. The iodine formed is used up at once by the thiosulfate, so no color appears until all the thiosulfate has gone, and then the starch turns blue-black.
The time to the color change, Δt, measures the initial rate: rate = [S₂O₃²⁻]₀ ÷ (2Δt), as each persulfate that reacts produces an iodine that uses up two thiosulfate.
Varying the initial concentrations of persulfate and iodide in turn and comparing the rates gives the orders (both are 1, so rate = k[S₂O₈²⁻][I⁻]).
Doing it at 4–5 temperatures gives Eₐ, typically about 50 kJ/mol.

sections.text: Temperature drift (a 1 °C change alters the rate by roughly 7%), a slow start (mixing time), judging the color change by eye, concentration errors, and iodide oxidation by air in old solutions.
Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of ethyl acetate, followed by titrating the acetic acid formed, and the inversion of sucrose followed by polarimetry.

quiz.q: In the crystal violet experiment, what plot gives a straight line when OH⁻ is in large excess?
What does the time to the color change in the iodine clock measure?
quiz.a: The initial rate of the reaction

entries.name: Experiment: conductivity of electrolytes and electrochemical cells
terms: temperature dependence of cell potential experiment
entries.tagline: Measuring how well solutions carry current, and what cell voltages tell you.

points: A conductivity cell has two platinum electrodes. The cell constant K_cell (in cm⁻¹) is found by measuring a standard of known conductivity, usually 0.01 M KCl (κ = 1.413 mS/cm at 25 °C). κ = K_cell × G, where G is the measured conductance.
An AC bridge at about 1 kHz is used, because DC would cause polarization at the electrodes.
Molar conductivity Λₘ = κ ÷ c.

sections.text: Kohlrausch's law. A plot of Λₘ against √c for KCl or NaCl is a straight line, and the intercept is the limiting molar conductivity Λ°. The law of independent migration of ions says Λ° = ν₊λ°₊ + ν₋λ°₋.

points: Λ° for acetic acid is found by adding the ionic values: 349.8 (H⁺) + 40.9 (CH₃COO⁻) = 390.7 S cm² mol⁻¹.
Degree of dissociation α = Λₘ ÷ Λ°.
Ka = cα² ÷ (1 − α) (Ostwald dilution law). The accepted value is 1.8 × 10⁻⁵.
A plot of 1/Λₘ against cΛₘ is linear, with slope 1/(KaΛ°²).
Build a Zn|Zn²⁺‖Cu²⁺|Cu cell with a salt bridge and measure E with a high-impedance voltmeter, so that no current flows.
Vary the concentration of one ion and plot E against log c. The Nernst slope is 59.2/n mV per decade, 29.6 mV for a 2-electron couple.
Measuring E at several temperatures gives (∂E/∂T), and so ΔS = nF(∂E/∂T) and ΔH = −nFE + nFT(∂E/∂T).

sections.text: Temperature (conductivity rises about 2% per °C), contamination of the water with CO₂ (which adds ions), electrode fouling, and, for cells, liquid junction potentials and concentration versus activity.

quiz.q: Why is an AC bridge used for conductivity measurements?
quiz.a: DC causes polarization at the electrodes

quiz.q: What does the degree of dissociation of a weak electrolyte equal?

entries.name: Experiment: adsorption isotherm (acetic acid on charcoal)
terms: adsorption of acetic acid on charcoal
entries.tagline: Measuring how much solute sticks to a solid surface and fitting an isotherm.

points: Weigh equal portions of activated charcoal into flasks. Add acetic acid solutions of different known concentrations, and shake at constant temperature until equilibrium is reached (30 minutes or more).
Filter, and titrate a sample of each filtrate with standardized NaOH, using phenolphthalein, to find the equilibrium concentration c.

sections.text: The amount adsorbed per gram is x/m = (c₀ − c) × V ÷ m, where c₀ is the initial concentration and V the volume of solution.

facts: x/m = k c^(1/n). A plot of log(x/m) against log c is straight, with slope 1/n and intercept log k. Empirical, and good for heterogeneous surfaces over a middle range.
c ÷ (x/m) = c ÷ (x/m)_max + 1 ÷ (K (x/m)_max). A plot of c/(x/m) against c is straight, with slope 1/(x/m)_max, the monolayer capacity.

sections.text: From the monolayer capacity, the surface area is (x/m)_max × N_A × the area of one adsorbed molecule (about 0.21 nm² for acetic acid), often of the order of several hundred m² per gram for activated charcoal.

Equilibrium not reached, adsorption of acid on the filter paper, absorption of CO₂ by the NaOH, the temperature drifting, and charcoal that has not been dried and degassed in the same way for each flask.

quiz.q: What does a plot of log(x/m) against log c give for a Freundlich isotherm?

entries.name: Experiment: viscosity and the molecular weight of a polymer
entries.tagline: Using how fast a polymer solution flows through a capillary to find the size of the chains.

sections.text: In an Ostwald viscometer, the time t for a fixed volume to flow through a capillary is proportional to η/ρ (Poiseuille's law). For dilute solutions, ρ is close to the solvent value, so relative viscosities are simply ratios of times.
[η] is the intrinsic viscosity, which measures the contribution of one polymer molecule.

points: Measure the flow time of the pure solvent and of several dilutions of the polymer solution, with the temperature controlled to ±0.05 °C.
Plot η_sp/c against c (Huggins) and ln(η_r)/c against c (Kraemer). Both lines extrapolate to the same intercept, [η].

The Mark–Houwink equation [η] = K Mᵃ links [η] to the molar mass M. K and a are constants for a given polymer, solvent and temperature, found from calibration with samples of known M. The exponent a is 0.5 for a random coil in a theta solvent, 0.5–0.8 in a good solvent and up to about 2 for stiff rods.

sections.text: Dust blocking the capillary, a viscometer that is not vertical, the temperature, drainage errors, and the kinetic energy correction at short flow times. Polymer samples have a distribution of chain lengths, so M is a viscosity average, M_v, which is between the number-average and weight-average.

quiz.q: What is the intrinsic viscosity?
quiz.a: The limit of η_sp/c as c approaches zero
wrong: The viscosity of the pure solvent

entries.name: Experiment: conjugated dyes and the particle in a box
entries.tagline: Testing the particle-in-a-box model on the colors of a series of dyes.

sections.text: The π electrons of a polymethine (cyanine) dye can be treated as free to move along the chain, a particle in a one-dimensional box of length L. The N π electrons fill the lowest N/2 levels. The lowest-energy absorption is from level N/2 to level N/2 + 1:
points: The box length is taken as L = (number of bonds along the chain + 1) × the C–C bond length, about 140 pm.
Each extra –CH=CH– unit adds two carbons and two electrons, and lengthens the box.

sections.text: Record the visible absorption spectra of a series of cyanine dyes with increasing chain length, for example 1,1′-diethyl-2,2′-cyanine, -carbocyanine and -dicarbocyanine, in ethanol, and find λ_max for each.

points: The λ_max rises by about 100 nm for each additional vinyl group: roughly 520, 605 and 705 nm for the three dyes mentioned.

Plot the observed λ_max against the calculated one, or against the chain length. The model gives the right trend and about the right size, usually within 10–20%, with deviations from the equal bond lengths (real chains have some bond alternation) and from the assumption of a constant potential along the chain, and end effects.
Fitting the data can also give an effective bond length.

sections.text: It is the same reason that long conjugated molecules such as β-carotene and the pigments in dyes and in vision are colored.

quiz.q: What happens to the λ_max of a conjugated dye as the chain gets longer?

entries.name: Experiment: rovibrational spectrum of HCl and DCl
entries.tagline: Measuring a bond length and a force constant from the infrared spectrum of a gas.

points: HCl gas is made, for example by dripping concentrated sulfuric acid onto sodium chloride, or taken from a lecture bottle. DCl is made by using D₂SO₄ and NaCl or D₂O with a chloride source. Use a fume hood.
The gas fills a gas cell (10 cm path, KBr or NaCl windows, kept dry), and a high-resolution FTIR spectrum is measured, from about 2600 to 3100 cm⁻¹ for HCl and 1900–2300 cm⁻¹ for DCl.
The windows are corroded by moisture and the gas is toxic, so the cell is purged and flushed carefully.
Assign the P and R branch lines, with a gap at the band origin (no Q branch).
Lines at ν̃ = ν̃₀ + (B₁ + B₀)m + (B₁ − B₀)m², with m = J + 1 for R and m = −J for P. Fit this to the line positions to find ν̃₀, B₀ and B₁.

H³⁵Cl: ν̃₀ about 2886 cm⁻¹, B₀ about 10.44 cm⁻¹ and B₁ about 10.14 cm⁻¹. B₁ < B₀, since the bond is longer in the excited vibrational state, so the lines get closer on the R side and further apart on the P side.
Bond length: r₀ = √(h ÷ 8π²cμB₀), about 128 pm (the equilibrium value, from B_e, is 127.5 pm).

Force constant: k = 4π²c²ν̃²μ, about 480–515 N/m. The band origin (2886 cm⁻¹) is lower than the harmonic frequency ωₑ (2991 cm⁻¹) because of anharmonicity, and the anharmonic correction is needed for the best value.
Each line is a doublet because of the two chlorine isotopes, ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl, in the ratio 3:1. The ³⁷Cl lines are a couple of wavenumbers lower, since the reduced mass is larger.

DCl has a band origin of about 2091 cm⁻¹, with the ratio to HCl of 0.72, close to the √(μ_HCl/μ_DCl) = 0.717 expected, and a smaller B (about 5.4 cm⁻¹), which means closely spaced lines. The bond length is almost the same, which confirms the Born–Oppenheimer approximation.

quiz.q: Why is B₁ smaller than B₀ in a rovibrational spectrum?
quiz.a: The average bond length is greater in the excited vibrational state

entries.name: Experiment: fluorescence quenching (Stern–Volmer)
entries.tagline: Using the loss of fluorescence to measure a quenching rate constant.

sections.text: A quencher Q that collides with the excited fluorophore reduces its fluorescence. F₀ and F are the intensities without and with the quencher, k_q is the bimolecular quenching rate constant and τ₀ the lifetime without the quencher.

points: Prepare quinine sulfate in dilute sulfuric acid (about 0.05 M), a standard fluorophore with a quantum yield of about 0.55 and a lifetime of about 19 ns.
Add increasing amounts of a quencher such as potassium chloride or iodide, keeping the quinine concentration and the ionic strength fixed.
Excite at about 350 nm and record the emission near 450 nm in a fluorimeter.
Plot F₀/F against [Q]. A straight line, with intercept 1, shows simple dynamic quenching, and the slope is K_SV.
k_q = K_SV/τ₀. A slope of about 200 M⁻¹ with τ₀ = 19 ns gives k_q about 10¹⁰ M⁻¹ s⁻¹, close to the diffusion limit, so nearly every collision quenches.
Upward curvature suggests both dynamic and static quenching. A lifetime measurement distinguishes them, since in dynamic quenching the lifetime falls in step with the intensity.

sections.text: The inner filter effect if the absorbance exceeds about 0.05, quenching by dissolved oxygen, photobleaching, a drifting lamp, and a change in the absorption of the quinine when the quencher is added.

quiz.q: What does the intercept of a Stern–Volmer plot of F₀/F against [Q] equal for simple quenching?

entries.name: Experiment: hydrogen emission spectrum and the Rydberg constant
entries.tagline: Measuring the Balmer lines and getting the Rydberg constant.

sections.text: The visible lines of hydrogen are the Balmer series, in which the electron falls to n = 2. R_H = 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ is the Rydberg constant for hydrogen.

points: A grating spectrometer (or a spectrograph with a CCD) is calibrated with a mercury lamp, whose lines are known: 404.7, 435.8, 546.1 and 577.0/579.1 nm.
Observe a hydrogen discharge tube and record the wavelengths of the Balmer lines: Hα 656.3 nm (n = 3), Hβ 486.1 nm (n = 4), Hγ 434.0 nm (n = 5) and Hδ 410.2 nm (n = 6).
With a diffraction grating of spacing d, the condition nλ = d sin θ gives the wavelength from the angle.
Plot 1/λ against (1/4 − 1/n²). The slope is R_H, about 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ and the line should pass through the origin.
Compare with the value for infinite nuclear mass, R_∞ = 1.0974 × 10⁷ m⁻¹. R_H = R_∞ × μ/mₑ, where μ is the reduced mass of the electron and proton, a factor of 0.99946.
With deuterium, the lines are shifted to slightly shorter wavelengths (about 0.18 nm for Hα) because the reduced mass is larger. This isotope shift led to the discovery of deuterium by Urey in 1931.

sections.text: Calibration errors, reading the angle or pixel position, an unresolved Hα–Dα pair or fine structure, and broad lines from pressure and Doppler broadening in the discharge.

quiz.q: What is the wavelength of the Hα line, the n = 3 → 2 transition of hydrogen?

entries.name: Experiment: Raman spectrum of carbon tetrachloride
entries.tagline: A tetrahedral molecule in Raman: shifts, symmetry and polarization.

sections.text: A laser (often 532 nm or 785 nm) is focused on liquid CCl₄ in a cell, and the scattered light is collected at 90° and passed through a spectrometer. Rayleigh scattering at the laser wavelength is blocked by a filter, and the weak Raman lines are recorded as shifts in cm⁻¹. CCl₄ is toxic, so handle it in a hood.

facts: The A₁ symmetric stretch (breathing mode). The strongest line, and highly polarized.
The T₂ bending mode. Depolarized. (A T₂ stretch is near 762–790 cm⁻¹.)

sections.text: Measured with a polarizer in the scattered beam, parallel or perpendicular to the polarization of the laser. Totally symmetric modes (A₁) give ρ < 3/4 and often close to 0 (about 0.01 for the 459 line). Non-symmetric modes give ρ = 3/4. This allows modes to be assigned by symmetry.

The 459 cm⁻¹ line shows a pattern of several peaks, from molecules with different combinations of ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl (the isotopes are in the ratio 3:1), since the frequency depends on the mass. They fall within a range of about 10 cm⁻¹, and the intensities follow the binomial statistics of the isotope mix.

Stokes lines (the molecule gains energy, the light loses it) appear at lower frequency than the laser. Anti-Stokes lines (from molecules already vibrationally excited) are at higher frequency, and weaker. Their intensity ratio follows the Boltzmann factor, e^(−hcν̃/kT), so it can give the temperature.

quiz.q: Which CCl₄ Raman line is strongly polarized?

entries.name: Experiment: heat capacity ratio of gases
entries.tagline: Measuring γ = C_p/C_V from an adiabatic expansion or the speed of sound.

sections.text: γ = C_p/C_V is about 1.67 for monatomic gases, 1.40 for diatomic gases at room temperature, and lower, about 1.3, for non-linear polyatomic molecules. It reflects the number of active degrees of freedom: γ = (f + 2)/f for f degrees of freedom.

points: A large flask is filled with the gas at slightly above atmospheric pressure, and the excess pressure h₁ is read on an oil manometer.
A stopcock is opened for a moment to let the pressure drop to atmospheric, a quick, nearly adiabatic expansion that cools the gas. The tap is closed.
The gas then warms back to room temperature at constant volume, and the pressure rises to a new excess h₂.
γ = h₁ ÷ (h₁ − h₂).

sections.text: A resonance tube or a speed-of-sound apparatus gives v from the frequency and the standing-wave wavelength, and γ = v²M/RT. The speed of sound is about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C and about 1007 m/s in helium.

The expansion is not perfectly adiabatic, heat exchange with the walls, the stopcock being open too long or too short, and moisture or impurity in the gas. For polyatomic gases, vibrational contributions make γ depend on temperature.

quiz.q: What value of γ is expected for a monatomic gas such as argon?
